questions.q: About how much water does a healthy adult gain per day in total from drinks, food and metabolism?
questions.explain: Roughly 1,200 mL from drinks, 1,000 mL from food and 350 mL produced by metabolism, about 2,550 mL a day. In balance, the same amount is lost.

open.q: About how much water does a healthy adult gain per day in total from drinks, food and metabolism?

questions.q: How much metabolic water does the body produce per day?
questions.explain: Oxidation of food produces about 350 mL of water a day, on top of drinks (about 1,200 mL) and food (about 1,000 mL).

open.q: How much metabolic water does the body produce per day?

questions.q: Which route accounts for the largest daily water loss in a healthy adult?
options: Insensible loss from skin and lungs
questions.explain: Urine is about 1,500 mL a day, insensible loss about 900 mL, faeces about 100 mL and sweat about 50 mL in normal conditions.

open.q: Which route accounts for the largest daily water loss in a healthy adult?

questions.q: What is meant by insensible water loss, and about how much is lost per day?
options: Sweating in hot weather, about 900 mL
Evaporation from skin and lungs, about 900 mL
Water lost in faeces, about 100 mL
Urine passed each day, about 1,500 mL
questions.explain: It is called insensible because it is not noticed. It continues even in cold weather and is separate from visible sweating.

open.q: What is meant by insensible water loss, and about how much is lost per day?

questions.q: What is the main route by which sodium leaves the body in health?
questions.explain: Nearly all sodium loss is through the kidneys. Sweat and faeces each lose only a small amount, so the kidney controls sodium balance.

open.q: What is the main route by which sodium leaves the body in health?

questions.q: Severe diarrhoea mainly causes loss of which of these?
questions.explain: Diarrhoea loses water and sodium, along with bicarbonate and potassium, which can lead to dehydration and metabolic acidosis.

open.q: Severe diarrhoea mainly causes loss of which substances from the body?

questions.q: Which condition causes loss of water alone, as very dilute urine?
questions.explain: Diabetes insipidus is a lack of ADH or of the kidney's response to it. Diabetes mellitus loses water and glucose, haemorrhage loses water and all electrolytes, and sweating loses water and sodium.

open.q: Which condition causes loss of water alone, as very dilute urine?

questions.q: Which of these is a cause of fluid overload (excess fluid gain)?
questions.explain: Fluid excess follows over-transfusion, over-hydration or excessive water drinking (polydipsia). The other options all lose fluid.

open.q: Name a cause of fluid overload (excess fluid gain).

questions.q: What mainly determines the volume of the extracellular fluid?
options: The total amount of sodium in the body
questions.explain: Sodium and its associated anions make up about 90% of ECF solute, so changes in total body sodium cause matching changes in ECF volume, which in turn drives the controls on sodium excretion.

open.q: What mainly determines the volume of the extracellular fluid?

questions.q: What is pressure natriuresis?
options: Increased sodium retention when arterial pressure rises
Increased sodium excretion when arterial pressure rises
Sodium loss caused by diuretic drugs
Increased potassium loss when pressure falls
questions.explain: A rise in arterial pressure acts directly on the tubules to reduce sodium reabsorption and also suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so more sodium and water are excreted and pressure returns toward normal.

open.q: What is pressure natriuresis?
accept: more sodium excreted when blood pressure rises
increased sodium excretion with raised blood pressure

questions.q: What happens to sodium excretion when arterial blood pressure falls?
options: It falls, because the renin-angiotensin system is stimulated and tubules retain sodium
It is unchanged, because blood pressure has no effect on how the kidney handles sodium
It rises, because aldosterone secretion is switched off when pressure drops
It rises, because the tubules reabsorb less sodium to lower the blood volume
questions.explain: A fall in pressure stimulates renin release and enhances sodium reabsorption directly in the tubules, so sodium and water are retained.

open.q: What happens to sodium excretion when arterial blood pressure falls, and why?

questions.q: Total body water in an average adult male is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.explain: Total body water is about 60% of body weight in an adult male and about 50% in an adult female, because females have more body fat.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of an average adult male's body weight is total body water?

questions.q: What fraction of total body water is intracellular fluid?
questions.explain: Intracellular fluid makes up about two-thirds of total body water and extracellular fluid about one-third.

open.q: What fraction of total body water lies inside cells?

questions.q: What fraction of the extracellular fluid is plasma?
questions.explain: Extracellular fluid is about one-quarter plasma and three-quarters interstitial fluid. Many students wrongly pick one-half.

open.q: What fraction of the extracellular fluid volume is plasma?

questions.q: Which is the major cation of the extracellular fluid?
questions.explain: Sodium is the principal extracellular cation and the main determinant of extracellular osmolality and volume. Potassium is the main intracellular cation.

open.q: Which is the major cation of the extracellular fluid?

questions.q: Which is the major cation of the intracellular fluid?
questions.explain: Potassium is concentrated inside cells, maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.

open.q: Which is the major cation of the intracellular fluid?

questions.q: Which is the major anion of the extracellular fluid?
questions.explain: Chloride is the most abundant extracellular anion, followed by bicarbonate. Phosphate and proteins are the main intracellular anions.

open.q: Which is the major anion of the extracellular fluid?

questions.q: What is the normal range of plasma osmolality?
questions.explain: Normal plasma osmolality is about 275 to 295 mOsm/kg, held in a narrow range mainly by ADH and thirst.

open.q: What is the normal range of plasma osmolality in mOsm/kg?

questions.q: Which Starling force mainly favours movement of fluid out of the capillary into the interstitium?
questions.explain: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of the capillary. Plasma oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in.

open.q: Which Starling force chiefly drives fluid out of the capillary into the interstitial space?

questions.q: From which structure is antidiuretic hormone (ADH) released into the circulation?
questions.explain: ADH is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

open.q: From which structure is ADH released into the blood after being synthesised in the hypothalamus?

questions.q: What is the main renal action of ADH?
options: Inserts aquaporin-1 into the proximal tubule
Inserts aquaporin-2 into collecting duct principal cells
Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Blocks the epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
questions.explain: ADH acts on V2 receptors and causes insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane of collecting duct principal cells, increasing water reabsorption.

open.q: Through which water channel, inserted in collecting duct principal cells, does ADH increase water reabsorption?

questions.q: Which is the most important physiological stimulus for ADH secretion?
questions.explain: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect a rise in plasma osmolality and stimulate ADH release. Large falls in blood volume or pressure also stimulate ADH.

open.q: What change in the blood is the most important physiological stimulus for ADH secretion?

questions.q: Aldosterone is secreted by which part of the adrenal gland?
questions.explain: The zona glomerulosa, the outermost zone of the cortex, secretes aldosterone. The fasciculata secretes cortisol and the reticularis secretes androgens.

open.q: Which zone of the adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone?
accept: Outermost zone of the adrenal cortex

questions.q: What is the effect of aldosterone on the distal nephron?
options: Increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
Decreases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
Increases both sodium and potassium reabsorption
Increases sodium excretion and potassium reabsorption
questions.explain: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. It promotes sodium retention and potassium loss.

open.q: What is the effect of aldosterone on sodium and potassium handling in the distal nephron?
accept: Raises Na reabsorption and K secretion

questions.q: Which cells of the kidney secrete renin?
options: Juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.explain: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole secrete renin. The macula densa senses distal tubular sodium chloride delivery and signals to them.

open.q: Which kidney cells, located in the wall of the afferent arteriole, secrete renin?

questions.q: What is the main renal effect of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)?
questions.explain: ANP is released when the atria are stretched by volume expansion. It promotes natriuresis and diuresis and inhibits renin and aldosterone.

open.q: What is the main effect of atrial natriuretic peptide on renal sodium handling?

questions.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered sodium?
questions.explain: The proximal tubule reabsorbs about 65% of filtered sodium and water. The thick ascending limb reabsorbs about 25%.

open.q: Which nephron segment reabsorbs the largest proportion of filtered sodium?

questions.q: Furosemide produces diuresis by inhibiting which transporter?
options: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, and amiloride blocks ENaC.

open.q: On which transporter, and in which nephron segment, does furosemide act?
accept: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.q: Which ECG finding is characteristic of hypokalaemia?
questions.explain: Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves. Tall peaked T waves occur in hyperkalaemia.

open.q: Which wave appearing after the T wave is characteristic of hypokalaemia on ECG?

questions.q: Which is the earliest ECG change in hyperkalaemia?
questions.explain: Tall tented T waves appear first. With rising potassium, the PR interval lengthens, P waves flatten and the QRS widens, which can progress to a sine wave pattern.

open.q: What is the earliest ECG change seen in hyperkalaemia?

questions.q: A patient with renal failure has a serum potassium of 7.2 mmol/L with tall peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which is the first immediate treatment to stabilise the myocardium?
questions.explain: IV calcium gluconate antagonises the effect of potassium on cardiac membranes and acts within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin with dextrose, salbutamol and later removal of potassium follow.

open.q: A patient with renal failure has a serum potassium of 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS. What is the first immediate drug treatment to stabilise the myocardium?

questions.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has serum sodium of 120 mmol/L, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and clinical euvolaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Ectopic ADH from the tumour causes SIADH, with water retention, dilutional hyponatraemia and euvolaemia. Diabetes insipidus gives dilute urine and hypernatraemia.

open.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has serum sodium of 120 mmol/L, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and clinical euvolaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.q: Which is the preferred first-line fluid for a child with diarrhoea and mild to moderate dehydration who can drink?
questions.explain: Oral rehydration solution uses sodium-glucose cotransport to drive water absorption. Plain water lacks sodium and juice is hyperosmolar, which can worsen diarrhoea.

open.q: What is the preferred first-line fluid for a child with diarrhoea and mild to moderate dehydration who can still drink?

questions.q: After a head injury a patient passes large volumes of dilute urine and has a serum sodium of 152 mmol/L. Deficiency of which hormone is most likely?
questions.explain: Damage to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary causes cranial diabetes insipidus. The kidneys cannot concentrate urine, leading to water loss and hypernatraemia.

open.q: After a head injury a patient passes large volumes of dilute urine and has a serum sodium of 152 mmol/L. Deficiency of which hormone is most likely?

questions.q: Which intravenous crystalloid is isotonic and stays mainly in the extracellular compartment?
questions.explain: 0.9% saline has an osmolality close to plasma, so it expands the extracellular fluid without shifting water into cells. 5% dextrose in water distributes across all compartments once the glucose is metabolised.

open.q: Which commonly used intravenous crystalloid is isotonic and stays mainly in the extracellular fluid?

questions.q: Carpopedal spasm with a positive Chvostek sign suggests which electrolyte disturbance?
questions.explain: Low ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing tetany, perioral paraesthesia and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs.

open.q: Which electrolyte disturbance causes carpopedal spasm and a positive Chvostek sign?

questions.q: A patient with severe diarrhoea loses hypotonic fluid and develops increased plasma osmolality. Which hormonal response helps conserve water?
questions.explain: An increase in plasma osmolality stimulates hypothalamic osmoreceptors, promoting thirst and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release. ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 insertion.

open.q: What happens to ADH secretion when plasma osmolality rises?
